t: Cairo grew from a chain of settlements, Babylon Fortress, Fustat, al-Askar and al-Qata'i, until the Fatimids built al-Qahira in 969 as a palace city and the later rulers opened it to the public.
Under the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad the city reached close to half a million people by 1340, then lost many in the Black Death and in the shift of the spice trade to the Cape route.
Under the Ottomans Cairo became a provincial capital, and under Muhammad Ali and Isma'il it was rebuilt in part on European lines, becoming the capital of modern Egypt.
dyk: In 1168 the Fatimid vizier Shawar set fire to Fustat so that the Crusader king Amalric could not take it. The fire did not destroy the city, but it began its decline, and Cairo took over its trade.
ev: Amr ibn al-As founds Fustat beside Babylon Fortress after the Muslim conquest
The Fatimids conquer Egypt and Jawhar al-Saqili founds the city that becomes Cairo
Power passes from the Ayyubids to the Mamluks
The Black Death strikes the city
The Ottomans conquer Egypt and Cairo becomes a provincial capital
The Cairo Fire destroys nearly 700 shops, cinemas, casinos and hotels in the Downtown

f.founded: 969, when the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah had his general Jawhar al-Saqili build a new fortified city northeast of Fustat; the caliph arrived in 973 and gave it its name
f.where: On the east bank of the Nile and two islands in it, just south of the point where the river leaves its desert valley and branches into the Delta, in northern Egypt
f.known: Fustat and the Fatimid foundation of al-Qahira; al-Azhar; Saladin's Citadel; the Mamluk sultans' mosques and madrasas; the Black Death of 1348; the Cairo Geniza; Isma'il's Downtown; Tahrir Square
f.today: Cairo is the capital and largest city of Egypt, with a metropolitan area of more than 22 million people.
